title: Three Tree Traversals: Prefix, Infix, Postfix Notations
description: A single ExprNode tree class with three traversal functions: to_prefix (preorder), to_infix (inorder with parens), to_postfix (postorder). Plus eval_tree (postorder evaluation). Two trees demonstrate how shape encodes precedence: (1+2)*3 has * at root, 1+2*3 has + at root with * deeper.

steps.description: ExprNode dataclass: value holds number, variable, or operator. left/right children optional. is_leaf returns True when both children are None.
to_prefix: preorder traversal. If leaf, return value. Otherwise return 'op left right' with recursive calls on children.
to_infix: inorder traversal. Leaf returns value. Internal node returns '(left op right)' with parentheses around every subexpression.
to_postfix: postorder traversal. Leaf returns value. Internal returns 'left right op' with children first.
eval_tree: postorder evaluation. Leaf converts value to float. Internal evaluates both children, then applies operator from ops dict.

steps.question: In tree2 (1 + 2 * 3), which operator is at the root and why?
steps.answer: + is at the root because * binds tighter, so the * subtree becomes the right child of +

steps.description: Two trees built manually: tree1 has * at root with + and 3 as children (for (1+2)*3). tree2 has + at root with 1 and * as children (for 1+2*3). Tree shape encodes precedence.
Output for tree1: prefix '* + 1 2 3', infix '((1 + 2) * 3)', postfix '1 2 + 3 *', value 9.0 OK. tree2: prefix '+ 1 * 2 3', infix '(1 + (2 * 3))', postfix '1 2 3 * +', value 7.0 OK.
